name: Lifecycle
one_liner: Four PM² phases stay; inside Executing the CIR cycles spin.
purpose: Projects pass through the same four distinct phases described by PM² — Initiating, Planning, Executing and Closing — and PM²-Agile keeps them. The phases are seldom cleanly separated: planning activities continue into Executing, and team-level tasks are not sequential at all, since planning, analysing, coding, testing and reviewing happen in every iteration. PM²-Agile then adds iterative cycles at three levels — daily cycles, iterations and releases — each following the CIR rhythm.
meta: Serial in the large, iterative in the small
Daily cycles · Iterations · Releases — all three run CIR
Seldom clearly separated; phase activities overlap (Figs. 3.6 & 3.8)
Iteration Planning under Planning; Stand-up, Review, Retrospective under Executing; Release Planning under Monitor & Control

items: Determine an overall vision; identify stakeholders and their success criteria
Declare all assumptions rather than treat them as facts, so they can be questioned
Identify the hypotheses that validate the assumptions and cut uncertainty risk early
Ascertain at least one solution and assess technical feasibility against those assumptions
Capture high-level estimates of cost, schedule and risk for the development aspect
Agile adds: Lean UX "Incept assumptions and research" co-creation sessions (§4.1, p. 28)
Artefacts: Business Case, Project Charter, Architecture Overview, Operational Model
Agile adds: Development Handbook — the tailoring record (created in Planning)
Agile adds: Development Work Plan — Work Items List, Release Plan, Iteration Plan
Hold the first Release Planning ceremony as early as possible, preferably at the start of Planning (p. 78)
Test Plan and Deployment Plan created
Appendix B.2 files the Iteration Planning meeting under the Planning phase (p. 95)
The focus shifts to incrementally building the solution and testing the hypotheses
Requirements are continuously revisited and clarified; technical and non-technical risks regularly addressed
Agile adds: Daily Stand-up, Iteration Review and Iteration Retrospective (App. B.2, p. 95)
Agile adds: Development Status Report, Retrospectives Log, Testing Logs
Design Blocks revisit hypotheses in every iteration to keep expectations aligned
Value is measured with a measuring-and-learning framework fed by an MVP

diagram.sec: 4. Closing — the phase does not disappear
items: Focus shifts to integrating the solution into the overall project deliverables
Ensure the organisation can own, evolve and maintain the information system after the project
Project-End Report: BM S · PM R · TeCo S · PrOw I · ArOw I · ATeM I (p. 95)
The Retrospectives Log becomes an invaluable source for the Lessons Learned (p. 57)
Planning-type activities peak in Planning but continue into later phases (Fig. 3.6)
Iterations create extensive overlap of phase activities over time (Fig. 3.8)
Team-level tasks are not sequential: plan, analyse, code, test and review every iteration
Some Agile practices reserve a special time slot for planning and reviewing

diagram.sec: 6. Three cycle levels, one rhythm (Fig. 3.10, p. 19)
items: Project phases → Releases → Iterations → Daily cycles
A release is the incremental progress of one or more iterations
An iteration's output is the incremental progress achieved every day
At all three levels value is delivered and feedback is collected

fields.what: All events and activities from inception of the idea or need through to final completion of the project, across four distinct phases.
fields.pollux: 04 Sep 2028 initiation request to 20 Mar 2030 administrative closure.

fields.what: Understand what to build: vision, stakeholders, success criteria, declared assumptions, hypotheses to test, at least one feasible solution, high-level estimates.
fields.who: BM R on the Business Case · PM R on the Charter
fields.pollux: Five measurable success criteria, from five days and four analysts down to one day, one analyst.

fields.what: Set up how delivery will run and at what detail: Development Handbook, Development Work Plan, Test Plan, Deployment Plan; first Release Plan built here.
fields.pollux: Handbook and Work Plan baselined 27 Nov 2028; RfE gate passed 04 Dec 2028.

fields.what: Iterations run the CIR rhythm and build the solution incrementally; artefacts are updated, not recreated; four of the five ceremonies live here.
fields.pollux: Iteration 1 begins 08 Jan 2029; twenty-six iterations to transition.

fields.what: Integrate the solution, transition ownership to the organisation, and capture Lessons Learned enriched by the iteration retrospectives.
fields.who: PM R on the Project-End Report
fields.pollux: Transition into service 31 Jan 2030; RfC gate 14 Feb 2030.

fields.what: Interfaces between phases are seldom clearly separated; planning-type activities continue to be executed during subsequent phases.
fields.pollux: Release Planning keeps replanning scope long after the Planning phase closed.

fields.f: Serial in the large, iterative in the small
fields.what: A driver (p. 23): the project has a defined beginning and end and a serial phase order, while team-level work inside iterations is not sequential.
fields.pollux: Gates are serial; the eleven-spreadsheet problem is attacked two weeks at a time.

fields.what: At the start uncertainty is high, so assumptions are declared and not treated as facts, giving stakeholders and team the chance to question them.
fields.pollux: "The Board wants one page" was recorded as an assumption, not a requirement.

fields.what: Each feature carries a hypothesis targeting the validation of a declared assumption, tested as development progresses.
fields.pollux: Hypothesis: a self-service view removes four of the eleven manual spreadsheets.

fields.what: A measuring-and-learning framework captures relevant data from an MVP or later versions and uses it as validated learning to enable decisions.
fields.pollux: Release 1 is read-only exposure by member state — the smallest thing worth using.

fields.what: Coordinate, Implement, Review: the pattern every cycle follows regardless of duration — daily cycles, iterations and releases.
fields.pollux: Coordinate at 09:30 stand-up, implement all day, review on the last Friday.

fields.what: Daily cycles nest inside iterations, iterations inside releases, releases inside phases. Value and feedback flow at every level.
fields.pollux: Daily stand-up · two-week iteration · quarterly release · 18-month project.

fields.what: Workshops, part of Release Planning, that use low- then high-fidelity prototypes to challenge requirements until common understanding is reached.
fields.who: ATeMs facilitate · PrOw presents to business
fields.pollux: Used before every Release 2 story so Risk and Finance argue over sketches, not code.

fields.what: The container of three plan levels — Work Items List, Release Plan, Iteration Plan — created in Planning and updated throughout Executing.
fields.who: TeCo R · PM A · PrOw S
fields.pollux: The answer to Gantt when he assumes an agile project has no schedule.

fields.what: The Coordination and Reporting artefact that carries development progress into the Project Status Report for the managing layer.
fields.pollux: Where the PM's status questions belong — not in the Daily Stand-up.

fields.what: A PM²-Agile Log holding the output of every Iteration Retrospective; feeds the Lessons Learned and post-project recommendations at Closing.
fields.who: TeCo R · PM A · ATeM S
fields.pollux: Eighteen months of retrospectives sit beside one Lessons Learned exercise.

fields.what: The summary table files Iteration Planning under Planning, Stand-up, Review and Retrospective under Executing, and Release Planning under Monitor & Control.
fields.pollux: Quoted in the POLLUX Development Handbook to settle where each ceremony reports.

fields.what: Architecture Overview is created in Initiating; Handbook, Work Plan, WIL, Release Plan, Test and Deployment Plans in Planning; all updated in Executing.
fields.pollux: Architecture Overview created before the RfP gate on 16 Oct 2028.

fields.what: PM² captures lessons at the end; PM²-Agile retrospects every iteration so improvements are acted on immediately rather than remembered later.
fields.pollux: Deming is delighted; someone still has to explain why both exist at Closing.

traps: Agile does not delete phases or gates — only the Executing work changes shape.
Appendix B.2 files Release Planning under Monitor & Control, not Planning.
Iteration Planning is filed under the Planning phase, though it runs every iteration.
Phases overlap; "planning ends when Planning ends" is false.
Retrospectives do not replace the Project-End Report or Lessons Learned.
